# Building and testing forge crates

Every forge repo depends on siblings by relative path. The working root already has the
correct flat layout — **always run cargo from inside the repo directory**, never from the root.

The facts in this skill — every per-repo command, every pinned number — are atom blocks
rendered from `forge-facts` at `harness build`, and the sweep checks each one against the
repo's own CI workflow. A block that reads wrong is a fact that moved: fix the atom (a new
version), never the prose here. `doctor` reports this skill stale when a pinned fact fails.

## Before you start

<!-- fact: platform/toolchain-pinned-1-95-0 -->
Every forge repo that carries a rust-toolchain.toml pins channel 1.95.0, except forge-platform-e2e, which says stable.

Every `forge-*/rust-toolchain.toml` in the working root pins `channel = "1.95.0"` (with rustfmt and clippy), so CI and local dev run the same lints. The one exception is the archived `forge-platform-e2e`, which says `stable`. Do not override the pin with `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`: a floating stable lands every new lint as a `-D warnings` failure.

Don't override with `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` — CI learned the hard way that "stable" silently
floats every new rustfmt/clippy lint into the build as `-D warnings`.

<!-- fact: platform/wasm-target-wasip1 -->
The wasm target is wasm32-wasip1: forge-runtime's CI installs it for its tests, and the guest repos declare it in rust-toolchain.toml.

The guest wasm target is `wasm32-wasip1`. forge-runtime's CI installs it (`targets: wasm32-wasip1`) because its tests build guest modules; `forge-sdk-v2-hello`, `forge-sdk-v2-storage-probe`, `forge-sdk-v2-test-fixtures`, `forge-lang`, `forge-connectors` and `forge-portal-web` declare it in their `rust-toolchain.toml`. Locally: `rustup target add wasm32-wasip1`.

- `--locked` everywhere. If it fails, the lockfile is genuinely out of date — say so rather
  than dropping the flag.

## Canonical commands, per repo

Run in this order; stop at the first failure. All commands assume `cd <repo>` first.

Each block below is the command set that repo's CI runs, verbatim, with the harness wrapper
token in front of every `cargo` subcommand but `fmt`. Where the emitted text shows a
`.harness/cargo` prefix, that repo is a **substrate** consumer: builds there run in a
flat-sibling worktree and take a per-lane lock.

Enrolled does not mean wrapped. Hybrid and customer consumers are enrolled — they
carry gates, fences and a `.harness/plan.json` — and they deliberately have no
wrapper (`harnesses/hybrid/harness.yaml` says so where the imports are declared).
The PATH shim knows: it asks `resolve-lane`, reads `wrap: false`, and execs the real
cargo. `forge-cli` is one of these, and a reader who goes looking for a
`.harness/cargo` there will not find one.

If a command is refused, the denial names the repair; don't reach for
`.harness/escapes.json` before reading it, and report a refusal that looks wrong
rather than working around it.

### `cargo` IS the harness now

<!-- fact: platform/cargo-shim-on-path -->
The cargo first on PATH is the harness shim at ~/.local/forge-harness/bin/cargo, which resolves the lane and execs its .harness/cargo wrapper.

`core/runner/lane-env.sh` puts `$HOME/.local/forge-harness/bin` first on `PATH`, and the root's `harness build` installs the shim (`core/runner/cargo-shim.sh`) there as `cargo`. The shim asks `dispatch.py resolve-lane --json` which consumer it is in and execs that lane's `.harness/cargo` wrapper with `cargo` prepended, so the lock, scratch env, build env and preflights apply to scripts and subprocesses too; a repo whose lane says `wrap: false` (hybrid consumers such as forge-cli) gets the real cargo. `cargo --version`, `cargo metadata` and `cargo fmt` pass straight through.

It refuses cargo in an unenrolled directory (D-043; escape `FORGE_HARNESS_UNGOVERNED=1`, recorded) and a substrate build in a main checkout, printing the `git worktree add` line.

In a lane, **`cargo test --tests --locked` just works**: the shim resolves which repo you
are in, then execs that lane's `.harness/cargo` with `cargo` prepended — the lock, the
scratch env, the build env and the preflights all still happen. `cargo --version`,
`cargo metadata` and `cargo fmt` go straight through, so a version probe no longer queues
behind somebody's twenty-minute build.

The explicit `.harness/cargo cargo …` form stays correct and is what CI runs; write
either. What the shim adds is that a *script*, a subprocess, or a peer's `bash -c` gets the
same treatment — it is the binary being invoked, not a guess at a command string. Two
things it refuses outright, from anywhere:

- **cargo in an unenrolled directory** (D-043). Escape: `FORGE_HARNESS_UNGOVERNED=1 cargo …`,
  recorded in `.harness/log/denials.jsonl` under fence `cargo-shim`.
- **a substrate build in a MAIN checkout** (D-027). The refusal prints the `git worktree add`
  line; there is no escape, because the worktree is the point.

One known bypass, documented rather than closed: calling `~/.cargo/bin/cargo` by absolute
path skips the shim. It is advisory-only — the session hook still warns on the text form —
and it is a deliberate hatch, not a loophole to reach for. If the shim is missing, stale or
edited, the hook goes back to a hard **deny** and tells you to run `harness install-shim`:
enforcement never quietly disappears with the enforcer.

### forge-runtime

Use the strings as written. A bare `cargo build` skips the server binary entirely and
produces an inert build, and deviating from the canonical feature string **re-resolves the
dependency graph**, which is how a stray build pulls in `openssl-sys` and spends minutes
compiling C that the canonical set never needed.

<!-- fact: platform/ci-commands-forge-runtime -->
forge-runtime's CI runs fmt, clippy --all-targets, build and test with --features adapters, then a no-default-features check and the api-smoke witness.

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked --features adapters -- -D warnings
cargo build --workspace --tests --locked --features adapters
FORGE_AUTH_CACHE_TTL_SECS=0 FORGE_DESIRED_STATE_CAS_ATTEMPTS=96 \
  cargo test --workspace --tests --no-fail-fast --locked --features adapters
cargo check --bin forge-runtime --locked --no-default-features --features adapters
bash -c 'cd examples/api-smoke && cargo check --locked'
```

- These are the steps `forge-runtime/.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs in `forge-runtime/`, after its grep fences (the legacy auth-carrier fence among them), in order.
- `--features adapters` is mandatory: a bare build skips the server binary and re-resolves the dependency graph.
- Clippy takes `--all-targets`, not `--tests`: `--tests` skips `examples/component_probe.rs`, which forge-lang's trace-diff oracle runs through.
- `FORGE_AUTH_CACHE_TTL_SECS=0` is required: the revocation and logout tests assert an instant `401 TOKEN_REVOKED`, which a cached verdict would hide. `FORGE_DESIRED_STATE_CAS_ATTEMPTS=96` gives the CAS-contention tests headroom on a loaded runner. CI also points `TMPDIR` at `$RUNNER_TEMP/forge-storage-tests` for the test step so the storage workspace template engages.
- The no-default-features check is the only tree that compiles the `not(jemalloc-stats)` arms; `examples/api-smoke` is the only witness for `pub` to `pub(crate)` demotions (baseline `tools/public-api-baseline.txt`).

### forge-storage

<!-- fact: platform/ci-commands-forge-storage -->
forge-storage's CI runs clippy with --workspace, the test suite with the chaos-tests tier, the member crates and a strict_mode pass, then three script gates.

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --tests --locked -- -D warnings
cargo build --tests --locked
cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast --locked --features chaos-tests
cargo test --workspace --exclude forge-storage --no-fail-fast --locked -F forge-storage-tx/chaos-tests
FORGE_STRICT_DECLARATIONS=1 cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast --locked strict_mode
./scripts/reachability-check.py
bash -c 'cd examples/embed-smoke && cargo check'
./scripts/ffi-guard-check.py
./scripts/verify-sdk-tsc.sh
```

- These are the steps `forge-storage/.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs in `forge-storage/`, in order.
- `--workspace` on clippy is load-bearing: without it the member crates compile as dependencies and their lints never fire.
- `chaos-tests` is the CI-only chaos/HA and slow tier (D-021), compile-gated behind the feature; a local run omits it. The member-crate step needs `-F forge-storage-tx/chaos-tests` because it excludes the root package, whose feature cannot reach there.
- The strict pass only exercises the reject paths with `FORGE_STRICT_DECLARATIONS=1`; tests must carry `strict_mode` in their name to be picked up.
- The test steps point `TMPDIR` at `$RUNNER_TEMP/forge-storage-tests`, and a template-proof step re-runs one test to show the storage template was reused.

### forge-agent

<!-- fact: platform/ci-commands-forge-agent -->
forge-agent's CI tests with --features chaos-tests and --test-threads=1, after fmt, clippy --tests and build --tests.

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --tests --locked -- -D warnings
cargo build --tests --locked
FORGE_AGENT_TEST_LISTEN_TIMEOUT_SECS=90 \
  cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast --locked --features chaos-tests -- --test-threads=1
```

- These are the steps `forge-agent/.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs in `forge-agent/`, in order.
- `--test-threads=1` is load-bearing: the e2e tests spawn full agent and mock-CP processes on fixed ports, and in parallel they collide.
- `--features chaos-tests` is the CI-only chaos/HA tier (D-021); a local run omits it.
- `FORGE_AGENT_TEST_LISTEN_TIMEOUT_SECS=90` raises the fixtures' 30 s listen floor under a loaded runner. CI reaps leaked `forge-mock-cp` and `target/debug/forge-agent` processes before the test step.

### forge-control-plane

<!-- fact: platform/ci-commands-forge-control-plane -->
forge-control-plane's CI checks fmt crate-scoped (cargo fmt -- --check) and tests with --test-threads=1.

```bash
cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy --tests --locked -- -D warnings
cargo build --tests --locked
FORGE_CP_TEST_LISTEN_TIMEOUT_SECS=120 \
  cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast --locked -- --test-threads=1
```

- These are the steps `forge-control-plane/.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs in `forge-control-plane/`, in order.
- fmt is scoped to this crate: `cargo fmt --all` resolves the whole path-dep tree through `cargo metadata`, reaching sibling workspaces (forge-web/core to forge-sdk-v2) that this CI does not check out.
- `--test-threads=1` is load-bearing: the integration suite spawns a full CP process per test, and in parallel one fails to bind.
- `FORGE_CP_TEST_LISTEN_TIMEOUT_SECS=120` raises the harness's 30 s listen floor for a slow cold bind. CI reaps orphaned `forge-control-plane` processes before the test step.

<!-- fact: platform/ci-commands-plain-crates -->
forge-edge, forge-secrets, forge-schema and forge-platform-wire run the same four CI commands: fmt --all, clippy --tests, build --tests, test --tests.

### forge-types

<!-- fact: platform/ci-commands-forge-types -->
forge-types' CI tests with cargo test --workspace and no --tests, so its doc-tests run.

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --tests --locked -- -D warnings
cargo build --tests --locked
cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast --locked
```

- These are the steps `forge-types/.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs, in order.

The test step drops `--tests` on purpose. forge-types is a virtual workspace, so cargo already covers every member; the target filter only excluded the doc-tests, and a doc example that stops compiling is the first sign a shared type's contract moved.

### forge-cli

<!-- fact: platform/ci-commands-forge-cli -->
forge-cli's CI scopes fmt, clippy and test to --package forge-cli, because --all drags in forge-web's workspace graph.

```bash
cargo fmt --package forge-cli -- --check
cargo clippy --package forge-cli --tests --locked -- -D warnings
cargo build --tests --locked
cargo test --package forge-cli --tests --no-fail-fast --locked
```

- These are the steps `forge-cli/.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs in `forge-cli/`, in order.

Package scoping is required: `--all` or `--workspace` resolves forge-web's whole workspace graph and fails.

### forge-platform-e2e

<!-- fact: platform/forge-platform-e2e-archived-no-ci -->
forge-platform-e2e has no ci.yml and no .harness/, only a .harness-exempt marker; its fmt, clippy, build and test commands live in e2e-pr.yml.

forge-platform-e2e is GitHub-archived. It carries no `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and no `.harness/` directory, only a `.harness-exempt` marker, so no gate or wrapper applies there. Its checks are in `.github/workflows/e2e-pr.yml`:

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --tests --locked -- -D warnings
cargo build --workspace --tests --locked
cargo test --workspace --tests --no-fail-fast --locked
```

It is also the one Rust repo whose `rust-toolchain.toml` says `stable` rather than `1.95.0`.

## Cost awareness

<!-- fact: platform/crate-line-counts -->
forge-runtime holds 204619 lines of tracked Rust and forge-storage 312255.

Both are genuinely slow from cold — tens of minutes. Prefer `cargo check` while iterating,
and set `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` to a stable path so the heavy unchanging deps stay compiled
between runs. Run long builds in the background rather than blocking.

**A rebuild is not free, and what triggers one is wider than it looks.** Touching a crate low
in the graph invalidates everything above it — editing `forge-capabilities` or
`forge-runtime-host` re-links `forge-adapters` and `forge-runtime`. So does `git stash` /
`git checkout`, which rewrites source mtimes across the tree. Both have turned a ~60s test
run into a ~10min wall clock.

### Do not rebuild to A/B a timing question

When the question is *"is this failure load-, order-, or timing-sensitive?"*, the binary is
the one thing that must stay fixed. Rebuilding between runs changes the artifact you were
trying to hold constant, and the timing you measure is mostly compilation.

Run the **existing** test binary directly instead:

```bash
# find it once, then re-run it as many times as the question needs
ls -t target/debug/deps/<test_name>-* | head -1
./target/debug/deps/<test_name>-<hash> --test-threads=1
```

Vary only the environment around it — thread count, competing load, ordering. Reserve
`cargo test` for when the code actually changed.

### A worktree does not isolate tests

Separate checkouts and separate `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`s isolate **compilation**. They do nothing
for fixtures that live outside the target dir, and `forge-storage`'s do:

<!-- fact: platform/forge-storage-test-root-seam -->
forge-storage's test anchor is $FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT, else $RUNNER_TEMP, else $HOME/.cache, each plus forge-storage-tests, and every test gets its own slot under it.

`anchor_opt()` in `crates/forge-storage-kernel/src/test_support.rs` picks the test anchor: `$FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT`, else `$RUNNER_TEMP`, else `$HOME/.cache`, each with `forge-storage-tests` appended. Dev machines export neither variable, so two processes on one machine share `$HOME/.cache/forge-storage-tests` unless the harness sets `FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT` per run (the `scratch_env` declaration does).

Inside the anchor, `test_root()` is per test: `<anchor>/<test slot>`, the slot built from the test thread's name and the pid, and `test_dir(prefix, name)` is `<test root>/<prefix>/<name>`, removed and re-created. Tests within one process no longer delete each other's data; the per-run root isolates processes.

Two concurrent runs therefore do not queue — `test_dir()` calls `remove_dir_all` before
`create_dir_all`, so each run **deletes the other's live data mid-test**. The
`workspace already locked by another process` flock error is the polite symptom; the silent
version is a suite that passes while reading another run's rows. That is not hypothetical:
it took down CI once, where 8 runners shared one user and `covering_index` saw every row
exactly twice (400/200, 600/300). CI never sees the bug because every GitHub runner exports
`RUNNER_TEMP`; dev machines export neither seam.

**You do not export it by hand.**

<!-- fact: platform/scratch-env-declared-for-storage -->
forge-storage and forge-lang declare scratch_env [FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT]; forge-runtime also declares TMPDIR=forge-storage-tests.

The per-run test scratch is declared once in each consumer's `.harness/consumer.yaml` as `scratch_env`, and both seams that invoke cargo (the wrapper and the runner's gate checks) point it at a fresh per-run directory and reap it afterwards; nobody exports it by hand.

- `forge-storage` and `forge-lang`: `scratch_env: [FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT]`
- `forge-runtime`: `scratch_env: [FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT, TMPDIR=forge-storage-tests]`

A bare `VAR` is the run root itself; `VAR=rel/subdir` is a subdirectory of it, created for the run. The TMPDIR form exists so a `TempDir` lands under `$FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT/forge-storage-tests`, where the storage workspace template engages.

Both seams that invoke cargo — the wrapper and the runner's own gate checks — point the
declared variable at a fresh per-run directory and reap it afterwards:

<!-- fact: platform/harness-run-root-on-disk-on-macos -->
On macOS the harness cargo wrapper puts its run root under $HOME/.cache/forge-harness-runs unless FORGE_HARNESS_SCRATCH_VOLUME names a volume.

`core/runner/cargo.sh` and `runner.py` resolve the run root to `$HOME/.cache/forge-harness-runs` on macOS unless `FORGE_HARNESS_SCRATCH_VOLUME` names a volume. A wedge can only happen to a volume someone mounted AND named.

So the isolated run is the ordinary one:

```bash
cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast --locked
```

A hand export is for the case the harness is not managing: bare `cargo` outside the wrapper,
or a repo that has not declared the variable yet. It is not the recommended form, and typing
it in front of a wrapped command only overrides a directory the wrapper already made:

```bash
FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT="$(mktemp -d)" cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast --locked
```

If a suite of yours anchors fixtures outside the target dir and the variable is NOT in
`scratch_env`, that declaration is the fix — not a line in your shell profile, which no
other session and no gate will ever see.

An entry has two shapes. Bare `VAR` is the run root itself. `VAR=rel/subdir` is a
subdirectory OF that root, created for the run and exported as `VAR`:

```yaml
scratch_env: [FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT, TMPDIR=forge-storage-tests]
```

The second form exists for the storage test template. `forge-storage` clones a prebuilt
workspace instead of bootstrapping one (~1 ms instead of ~1.5 s), and the clone fires only
when a workspace's `data_directory` starts with `$FORGE_STORAGE_TEST_ROOT/forge-storage-tests`
— the root itself does not qualify. A `TempDir` under `TMPDIR` reaches that check only if
`TMPDIR` IS that subdirectory, and the declaration above is how both seams make it so, with
the same per-run isolation and the same reaping as the bare form. An absolute path or a
`..` segment is refused at `harness build`, naming the entry: either would point the
variable outside the private root, which is the shared-fixture bug this block exists to
prevent.

**Serializing builds does not substitute for this.** They solve different problems: a lock
makes runs sequential, isolation makes them independent. Gate-internal cargo does not take
the build lock at all, so two suites can still overlap there — and for a suite anchored
outside the target dir, overlapping means corruption rather than contention.

### One target dir, one cargo at a time

Two concurrent cargo invocations against the same `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` do not politely queue.
They can fail with a **missing-rlib error that reads exactly like a code error** — a
compilation failure naming a dependency that is in fact fine — and the obvious response is to
go debug source that was never broken. If you need a genuine before/after comparison, give
each run its own `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` rather than interleaving them in one.

## Start a warm watcher in the lane you are working in

The gates pull today: you edit, the hook fires, the gate compiles, you wait. A **watcher**
pushes instead — it runs the same gates on every save and publishes each verdict under the
fileset fingerprint it was computed for, so by the time the hook fires the answer usually
already exists. Measured on a fixture whose gate takes 3 s: post-edit falls from ~3.4 s to
~30 ms.

**It moves the wait; it does not shorten it.** The watcher runs the same suite the hook
would. In a repo whose full suite takes twenty minutes (forge-lang: 1605 tests, a watcher's
full pass measured at 1,319 s on 2026-09-27) a pass can be superseded by the next edit before
anything adopts it, and it holds the build lock while it compiles. It is not the mitigation
for a Stop that cannot fit its suite — that is the Stop ceiling (G-11): pre-done runs under
what is left of the 1200 s Stop budget, and a gate whose recorded cost cannot fit is deferred
to the step commit with the reason in evidence. A watcher still pays where the suite is
minutes, not tens of minutes.

```bash
cd <repo-or-worktree>
python3 .harness/runner.py watch &        # one per lane; leave it running
python3 .harness/runner.py watch --status # what it holds, and how old
python3 .harness/runner.py watch --once   # one pass, then exit
```

It watches the consumer with `watchexec` when that is installed and falls back to a 1 s
poll otherwise — which one is in use is in the status output, never guessed at.

<!-- fact: platform/macbook-toolchain-state -->
The MacBook's dev tools are direct installs in ~/.local/bin (gh, yq, age, sops 3.12.2, watchexec) plus rustup, with Homebrew present since 2026-08-16.

Installed 2026-08-03 while getting the forge platform building and running locally. **As of 2026-08-08 there was no Homebrew on this machine** — everything was a direct binary install.

**Correction 2026-08-16: Homebrew is now present.** Seen via `/opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.14/...` in a pipx build error (a `python@3.14` formula is installed). Separately, a peer session reported `python3` also resolves to 3.14.7 via a **python.org** installer (additive, `/usr/bin/python3` untouched) — so there are two independent Python 3.14 installs on this machine (Homebrew's and python.org's), neither is the system one. The python.org build doesn't link the system trust store, which threw `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` on urllib/pip/requests until `Install Certificates.command` was run (already fixed, durable). Don't assume `brew install X` still fails — check first (`which brew`) rather than trusting the old "no Homebrew" claim.

| Tool | Version | Location |
|---|---|---|
| git | 2.50.1 (Apple) | via Xcode Command Line Tools |
| rustup / cargo / rustc | 1.97.1 stable | `~/.cargo/bin` |
| node / npx | 22.23.2 (since 2026-08-08; was 24.18.1 at `~/.local/node/bin`) | `~/.local/bin` |
| gh | 2.97.0 | `~/.local/bin` (pre-existing) |
| yq | 4.53.3 | `~/.local/bin` |
| age / age-keygen | 1.3.1 | `~/.local/bin` |
| sops | **3.12.2** | `~/.local/bin` |
| watchexec | 2.5.1 | `~/.local/bin` |

`~/.local/bin` is already on PATH. `~/.cargo/bin` and `~/.local/node/bin` may need exporting in non-login shells.

**Why:** sops is pinned to 3.12.2 deliberately — that is the version `bootstrap-node.sh` installs on the nodes, and the operator laptop encrypts what the node decrypts. Bump both together or not at all. Node was needed for `forge-platform-architecture/graph/tools/*.mjs` (fleet-check, render-map); Rust toolchains for the repos are pinned separately (`forge-runtime` and `forge-storage` pin 1.95.0 via `rust-toolchain.toml`, which rustup fetches on demand).

**How to apply:** before telling Rory to install something, check whether it is already here. See [[forge-local-dev-harness]].

**E2e runs locally now (2026-08-08):** node/npx on this machine means the
forge-portal-e2e Playwright suite no longer has to round-trip through CI on
forge-home — boot `dev/up-full.sh` and run `npx playwright test` (or a
single spec with `-g`) directly against the local platform. CI dispatch
remains the merge-boundary gate; local is for iteration. See
[[portal-e2e-ci-green]], [[forge-sdlc-harness-project]].

**Hardware (per Rory, 2026-08-15): 16 CPUs, 128 GB RAM.** Treat it as a small build farm — 4–6 concurrent build lanes are realistic if each gets a job budget (~16/lanes); RAM is not the constraint. See [[harness-roadmap-plan]] H-7 lanes.

**JAVA_HOME (2026-09-06, HC-12):** the Homebrew JDK is keg-only; `javac` on PATH is the macOS shim and exits 1 ("Unable to locate a Java Runtime"); JAVA_HOME is unset in the driver's shell. forge-lang's resolver reaches the keg on its own, but the HC-12 toolchain probe (and so the HC-1 verdict key for forge-lang) needs `export JAVA_HOME=/opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk` in the shell the driver starts from, or every forge-lang wake prints `verdict key unavailable: toolchain javac` and records nothing.
 Results land in `.harness/state/watch/`: one `<gate>.json` per watched gate plus
an `alive.json` heartbeat, refreshed every 5 s and **removed when the watcher exits**.

**What the hook does with it.** Before running a memoizing gate at post-edit or pre-done, the
runner compares its own fingerprint against the published one.

<!-- fact: platform/watcher-adoption-stale-seconds -->
The hook adopts a watcher's published gate verdict only while its heartbeat is younger than watch_stale_seconds, default 30.

`python3 .harness/runner.py watch` runs the plan's `watch_gates` (cargo-fmt, cargo-check, cargo-tests in the substrate plans) on every save and publishes each verdict under the fileset fingerprint it was computed for, in `.harness/state/watch/`, with an `alive.json` heartbeat refreshed every 5 s. At post-edit and pre-done the runner adopts a published verdict only when the fingerprint matches, the heartbeat is younger than `watch_stale_seconds` (30, from the plan, else `WATCH_STALE_SECONDS` in `core/runner/runner.py`) and the watcher's pid is alive; otherwise it runs the gate live and records `absent`, `stale`, `mismatch` or `dead`. An adopted fail blocks like a live one. Nothing starts a watcher for you.

Otherwise it runs the gate live and records why in the evidence entry — `absent`, `stale`,
`mismatch` or `dead`. There is no fourth outcome and no silent one: a gate that did not run
never looks like a gate that passed.

An adopted **fail** blocks exactly as a live fail would, with the watcher's own output as the
repair text. What adoption saves is the rebuild, never the failure. A check that could not
*run* publishes nothing at all — an infrastructure error is about the watcher's environment,
not about your tree, so the hook runs the gate live and reports its own.

Three things worth knowing before you rely on it:

- **Nothing starts it for you.** Hooks do not spawn watchers — a hook that starts daemons is
  a surprise — so a lane without one simply runs gates the old way.
- **Its builds take the build lock**, through `.harness/cargo` like everything else, so while
  the watcher is compiling a hook-side live run queues behind it (visible in
  `.harness/log/lock.jsonl`). That is the v0 trade: per-lane locks are what fix it.
- **`--once` is for tests and one-off checks.** It leaves a heartbeat behind but its process
  is gone, and adoption requires a live PID — so a `--once` run from a shell answers nothing
  afterwards.

Which gates it runs is `watch_gates` in `.harness/plan.json` (`cargo-fmt`, `cargo-check`,
`cargo-tests`). A named gate that is not in the consumer's plan, or that does not memoize,
is reported as a note when the watcher starts rather than watched silently.

## When a fence fails

`forge-runtime` CI has grep-based fences (e.g. the legacy auth-carrier fence) that run
*before* fmt/clippy/build/test. They have broken by matching nothing after a file move,
killing the job in ~40s and letting real regressions through unnoticed for weeks.

If CI fails at a fence: first confirm the pathspec still matches the tree
(`git grep -l <pattern> -- <pathspec>`). A fence that matches nothing is a broken gate,
not a clean run.

## Model tiering: delegate the typing, keep the judgment

The fleet emits a `forge-implementer` agent (Opus tier) into every consumer. The
implementation loop — tool results, build output, test output, edit iterations — is where
token volume concentrates, and it neither needs nor benefits from the orchestrating
session's model tier. Delegation also keeps that bulk out of the orchestrator's context.

- **Delegate** sizeable, self-contained implementation chunks: a multi-file change you have
  already specified, a mechanical migration across a crate, test-writing against a fixed
  behavior. Brief it completely the first time — repo, files, the change, constraints, the
  exact test command — and commit to the delegation: never redo or re-derive its work.
- **Keep in the main loop**: specification, review, verification of the implementer's
  output, debugging judgment, and anything under a handful of edits — delegation overhead
  (briefing, context re-establishment, report reading) exceeds the savings there.
- **Never delegate verification.** The implementer reports evidence; judging it is the
  orchestrator's job. Cap parallel implementers at 4 unless the work is genuinely
  independent and sizeable.

## sccache: don't probe stats with a bare invocation

<!-- fact: platform/harness-sccache-wired -->
The substrate harness declares RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache in build_env, so harness-driven cargo goes through sccache without it appearing on the command line.

The substrate harness declares `build_env: {RUSTC_WRAPPER: sccache, SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE: 25G}`
once in `forge-sdlc-harness/harnesses/substrate/harness.yaml` (D-031). Every consumer's
emitted `.harness/build-lock` exports it before taking the lock, and `runner.py`'s gate
path applies the same `build_env` — so all harness-driven cargo goes through sccache
**without it ever appearing on the command line**. Verified 2026-08-15: ~18G cache at
`~/Library/Caches/Mozilla.sccache`, live hits confirmed.

Gotchas:
- Registry deps (wasmtime etc.) hit across worktrees; local path crates mostly miss
  (absolute paths in args/debuginfo). Worktree cold builds still paying for local crates
  is expected, not evidence sccache is off. Do NOT add `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`.
- The server inherits its env (cache-size cap) from whichever invocation starts it.
  A bare `sccache --show-stats` starts one with the default 10 GiB cap, which would
  evict half the cache on the next write — check stats only when a server is already
  running, or set `SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE=25G` when doing so.
- A missing sccache binary degrades gracefully: build-lock unsets RUSTC_WRAPPER and
  warns; the build is slower, not broken.

See [[forge-build-lock-contention]] for the lock itself; the CI box has its own
separate sccache ([[forge-home-runner-box]]).

<!-- fact: platform/sccache-cache-size-declared-25g -->
The substrate and hybrid harnesses declare SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE: 25G, and a size already in the environment wins, which lane-env.sh sets to 100G on this Mac.

`build_env` in `harnesses/substrate/harness.yaml` and `harnesses/hybrid/harness.yaml` declares `SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE: 25G`, the CI-safe figure for forge-home's disk. The wrapper treats an `SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE` already in the environment as authoritative and records which it used as `sccache_size_from` (`machine`, `declared` or `unset`) in the lock log. `core/runner/lane-env.sh`, sourced from the shell profile, exports `SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE=100G` for this machine, where per-lane target dirs filled 25G.

A running sccache server keeps the cap it started with; restart it by hand with nothing compiling: `sccache --stop-server && SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE=100G sccache --start-server`.

It never appears on the command line, so its absence from a command proves nothing.
A bare `sccache --show-stats` **starts a server with the default 10 GiB cap** if none is
running, and that server will evict more than half the fleet cache on its next write.
Probe stats only when a wrapper-started server is already running, or prefix the
probe with the size you actually want.

### On this Mac: `SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE=100G`

25G is the **CI-safe** number — forge-home reached 82% disk on accumulated build dirs, and
that constraint has not changed. This machine is not forge-home: per-lane target dirs mean
several worktrees' worth of artefacts in one cache, and 25G is already full (measured
2026-08-16: `cache_size` 26,843,295,906 of `max_cache_size` 26,843,545,600 — 99.999%). A
cache at its cap is an eviction treadmill: it reads as a low hit rate and looks like the
cache not helping, when it is the cache being too small.

So the **machine wins**. The wrapper treats an `SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE` already in the
environment as authoritative and does not overwrite it with the declared 25G; the lock
record says which it used (`sccache_size_from`: `machine` | `declared` | `unset`).

Source `core/runner/lane-env.sh` from your shell profile, or export the same line:

```sh
export SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE=100G
```

A **running server keeps the cap it was started with.** Changing the env changes nothing
until it restarts, so a 100G profile and a 10G server look identical from outside. The
wrapper prints once per lane when the two disagree and never restarts the server itself —
killing one mid-build fails that build. Fix it by hand, with nothing compiling:

```sh
sccache --stop-server && SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE=100G sccache --start-server
```

## Lanes: locks, job budgets and path remapping

A **lane is a worktree**. The build lock is per lane (`lock_scope: consumer`, keyed on the
worktree basename), so `forge-storage--a` and `forge-storage--b` build at the same time
instead of queueing: their target dirs are separate by construction and sccache dedups the
compile work between them.

Because they run at once, the wrapper carves the CPU rather than letting each lane ask for
all of it.

<!-- fact: platform/lane-job-budget-clamp -->
Each lane builds under its own lock, and the wrapper sets CARGO_BUILD_JOBS and NEXTEST_TEST_THREADS to clamp(cores / active lanes, 4, cores) unless the caller set them.

A lane is a worktree. The substrate-build-isolation fence declares `lock_scope: consumer`, so the wrapper keys the build lock on the worktree basename and `forge-storage--a` and `forge-storage--b` build at once. Because they do, `core/runner/cargo.sh` carves the CPU after taking the lock: `JOBS = cores / active lanes` (active meaning holding a build lock or running a watcher), floored at 4 and capped at the core count, exported as `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` and `NEXTEST_TEST_THREADS`. A value the caller already set wins and is recorded as `jobs_from: caller` in `.harness/log/lock.jsonl` beside `active_lanes`.

**Set either variable yourself and yours wins**, recorded as `jobs_from: caller` in
`.harness/log/lock.jsonl` alongside `active_lanes`.

<!-- fact: platform/remap-path-prefix-in-lanes -->
The cargo wrapper appends --remap-path-prefix=<lane>=/forge/<repo> to RUSTFLAGS so a worktree's path stays out of the sccache key.

`core/runner/cargo.sh` appends `--remap-path-prefix=<lane root>=/forge/<repo>` to `RUSTFLAGS`, the repo name being the worktree basename before its `--`. Without it every worktree's absolute path reaches the sccache key and our own crates recompile cold in each lane. It appends, so a caller's `RUSTFLAGS` survives, and a caller who already remapped that prefix is left alone. Sibling path-deps are not remapped: they resolve to the same main-checkout path from every lane.

It **appends**; your `RUSTFLAGS` survives.
